claims.text: The initial material is a relaxed, single-crystal FCC FeNiCrCoCu coating on a single-crystal Cu matrix at 300 K.
Nanoindentation is performed to 30 Å at 10 m/s and at 300, 600, 900, and 1200 K.
Above 900 K, plasticity transitions from dislocation-mediated deformation to rapid lattice disordering and incipient amorphization.
Thermal activation overcomes a stacking-fault-energy barrier and drives the transition to lattice disordering.
At 300–600 K, dislocation nucleation and multiplication produce high hardness and are consistent with dislocation starvation in the small deformation volume.
Near 900 K, thermal energy facilitates stacking-fault annihilation and dislocation cross-slip.
Stacking-fault annihilation and cross-slip reduce dislocation density and elastic modulus near 900 K.
High temperature combined with the 10 m/s loading rate causes cascading disorder and loss of long-range FCC order.
The high loading rate prevents full recovery and thereby causes local structural disorder to accumulate.
Loss of crystalline order sharply reduces shear strength, hardness, and load-bearing capacity.
Reduced load-bearing capacity increases indentation depth and contact area, which raises the friction coefficient.
An amorphous-like tribolayer adheres to the Cu counterface and increases adhesive wear and friction.
The proposed mechanism is distinct from mechanical annealing because disorder is produced by coupled thermal agitation and high-rate loading rather than time-dependent recovery.
At 300 K and 600 K, the friction coefficient remains below 0.2 while hardness remains high.
At 900 K, the friction coefficient exceeds 0.4 and the wear rate increases by an order of magnitude because lattice disordering begins.
At 1200 K, extensive amorphization produces near-complete hardness loss and a friction coefficient above 0.6.
The sharp disordering transition is specific to single-crystal FeNiCrCoCu loaded at 10 m/s and may not occur in polycrystals or at lower rates.
Increasing the stacking-fault-energy barrier in a modified interatomic potential will selectively suppress lattice disordering.
HCP atom count, dislocation line length, and RDF can distinguish lattice disordering from mechanical annealing.
The cited FeNiCrCoCu simulation evidence reaches 900 K but does not establish an amorphization threshold above 900 K.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says reduced dislocation density is accompanied by reduced elastic modulus and attributes this to the query, whereas the query states that the dislocation-density decrease at 600 K increases elastic modulus.
The causal transition and friction spike are repeatedly placed above 900 K, but the predicted outcome states that the spike and order-of-magnitude wear increase already occur at exactly 900 K.
